options.a: Possible right mainstem intubation—pull the tube back 2 cm
options.b: Possible pleural effusion—schedule a chest X-ray for the morning
options.c: Possible pulmonary embolism—start a heparin drip right away
options.d: Possible pneumothorax—assess and notify the team urgently

distractorExplanations.a: Mainstem intubation follows tube placement; a sudden unilateral loss after a central line points to an iatrogenic pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.b: Effusion develops gradually with dull, diminished sounds; a sudden post-line desaturation needs urgent action, not a morning film.
distractorExplanations.c: PE usually leaves breath sounds present; unilateral absent sounds right after line placement point to pneumothorax.

options.a: Decreased compliance or increased airway resistance
options.b: Increased compliance from improving lung recruitment
options.c: A leak in the circuit or around the ETT cuff
options.d: Auto-triggering from an overly sensitive trigger setting

distractorExplanations.b: Higher compliance lowers the pressure needed for the same tidal volume, so PIP would fall, not rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaks lower circuit pressures and trigger low-pressure or low-volume alarms rather than a rising PIP.
distractorExplanations.d: Auto-triggering raises the breath rate; it does not raise the peak pressure of each breath at the same tidal volume.

options.a: Airway resistance, measured as the pressure at peak inspiratory flow
options.b: Alveolar pressure related to tidal volume and respiratory system compliance
options.c: Intrinsic PEEP, measured with an end-expiratory hold maneuver
options.d: Transpulmonary pressure, measured with an esophageal balloon catheter

distractorExplanations.a: Resistance is reflected by PIP minus Pplat; Pplat is taken during a no-flow inspiratory hold and reflects alveolar pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Auto-PEEP is measured with an expiratory hold; plateau pressure uses an end-inspiratory hold.
distractorExplanations.d: Pplat reflects the whole respiratory system; transpulmonary pressure needs esophageal pressure to subtract the chest wall.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-patient-data-00.explanation: Inspiratory hold (zero flow) yields Pplat used for compliance and lung-protective limits. It is measured during an inspiratory hold with no flow.

options.a: A low PaO2 on the ABG that confirms the degree of CO poisoning
options.b: A low SpO2 reading, because pulse oximeters detect COHb as deoxyhemoglobin
options.c: Normal or high SpO2 readings that do not reflect true oxygen content
options.d: Cyanosis that worsens in proportion to the measured COHb level

distractorExplanations.a: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen and is often normal in CO poisoning; it does not measure COHb.
distractorExplanations.b: Standard two-wavelength oximeters read COHb as oxyhemoglobin, giving a falsely normal or high SpO2, not a low one.
distractorExplanations.d: COHb does not cause cyanosis in proportion to its level; cyanosis is an unreliable sign in CO poisoning.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-patient-data-00.explanation: Standard SpO2 cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin; CO-oximetry measures COHb. Use CO-oximetry to measure COHb.

options.a: Pneumothorax, which causes dull percussion over the area
options.b: Pleural effusion, which causes bronchial breath sounds
options.c: Emphysema, which causes dull percussion and bronchial sounds
options.d: Consolidation (e.g., pneumonia) more than pneumothorax

distractorExplanations.a: Pneumothorax gives hyperresonance with absent or diminished breath sounds, not dullness with bronchial sounds.
distractorExplanations.b: Effusion is dull to percussion but breath sounds are diminished or absent over the fluid, not bronchial.
distractorExplanations.c: Emphysema causes hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds from air trapping, not consolidation findings.

options.a: Adequate oxygenation, hemodynamic stability, and resolution of the indication for ventilation
options.b: Adequate oxygenation on FiO2 0.60 with PEEP 12 cm H2O, plus a stable heart rate and blood pressure
options.c: A rapid shallow breathing index above 105 with stable blood pressure
options.d: Stable hemodynamics on escalating vasopressors and an improving chest X-ray

distractorExplanations.b: Readiness screens usually require FiO2 of about 0.40-0.50 or less and PEEP of about 5-8 cm H2O, not 0.60 and 12.
distractorExplanations.c: An RSBI below 105 predicts weaning success; a value above 105 predicts failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Escalating vasopressor doses mean the patient is not hemodynamically stable enough for a breathing trial.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-patient-data-00.explanation: Liberation readiness requires gas exchange and clinical stability sufficient to trial spontaneous breathing. These are screened conceptually before the trial.

options.a: Left ventricular failure with acute pulmonary edema
options.b: Tension pneumothorax compressing the great veins
options.c: Cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension complications
options.d: Superior vena cava syndrome from a lung tumor

distractorExplanations.a: LV failure presents with crackles and orthopnea; JVD, pedal edema, and a loud P2 in COPD point to right heart strain.
distractorExplanations.b: Tension pneumothorax is acute with absent breath sounds and tracheal shift, not chronic edema with a loud P2.
distractorExplanations.d: SVC syndrome causes facial and arm swelling with upper-body vein distension, not pedal edema with a loud P2.

options.a: Gradual hypoventilation from oversedation, a lower set rate, or respiratory muscle fatigue
options.b: Hyperventilation from pain, anxiety, or an increased set rate on the ventilator
options.c: Rebreathing from an exhausted CO2 absorber or a faulty expiratory valve in the circuit
options.d: Circuit disconnection, esophageal intubation, or catastrophic drop in pulmonary blood flow

distractorExplanations.a: Hypoventilation raises ETCO2 gradually; a sudden drop to near zero means CO2 is no longer reaching the sensor.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperventilation lowers ETCO2 gradually over minutes; it does not drop it abruptly to near zero.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebreathing raises the inspired CO2 baseline above zero; it does not cause a sudden fall to near zero.

options.a: Rising VC/NIF values signal the onset of respiratory muscle weakness
options.b: Declining VC/NIF can signal impending ventilatory failure
options.c: These tests detect hypoxemia earlier than pulse oximetry does
options.d: Intubation is indicated once VC falls below 40 mL/kg

distractorExplanations.a: Weakness lowers VC and makes NIF less negative; rising values mean improving strength.
distractorExplanations.c: VC and NIF measure respiratory muscle strength; hypoxemia is a late sign in neuromuscular failure.
distractorExplanations.d: The usual warning threshold is a VC of about 15-20 mL/kg; 40 mL/kg is still well above the danger zone.

options.a: Cherry-red skin with a falsely normal SpO2 near 100 percent
options.b: Low PaO2 on the ABG that rises once supplemental O2 is added
options.c: Cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood with SpO2/PaO2 discrepancies
options.d: Pink skin and normal SpO2, since MetHb carries oxygen normally

distractorExplanations.a: That classic (if unreliable) picture belongs to CO poisoning; methemoglobinemia gives cyanosis and SpO2 near 85 percent.
distractorExplanations.b: PaO2 is usually normal in methemoglobinemia; the defect is hemoglobin's inability to carry oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: Methemoglobin's ferric iron cannot bind oxygen and shifts the curve left, so content and delivery fall.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-patient-data-01.explanation: MetHb impairs oxygen delivery; methylene blue may be used clinically—diagnosis needs CO-oximetry. Confirm with CO-oximetry.

options.a: Checking solution volume, connections, gas flow, and for clogs
options.b: Increasing the flow to 15 L/min to force out more aerosol
options.c: Adding more saline diluent until the treatment lasts 30 minutes
options.d: Replacing the medication with an MDI because the drug has degraded

distractorExplanations.b: Running far above the specified 6-8 L/min increases aerosol loss and does not fix a clog, leak, or empty cup.
distractorExplanations.c: Sputtering often means the cup is near empty or faulty; stretching the treatment with diluent does not fix it.
distractorExplanations.d: Drug degradation does not make a nebulizer sputter; the cause is volume, connections, gas flow, or a clog.

options.a: Recalibrating the pulse oximeter, since the SpO2 reading is drifting
options.b: Verification with an oxygen analyzer and troubleshooting gas supplies/blender
options.c: Raising the set FiO2 dial until the patient's SpO2 returns to the ordered target range
options.d: Replacing the flowmeter, since blenders cannot fail once calibrated

distractorExplanations.a: A pulse oximeter measures patient saturation, not delivered FiO2; the blender output needs an oxygen analyzer.
distractorExplanations.c: Compensating with the dial masks a failing blender; delivered FiO2 must be verified with an analyzer.
distractorExplanations.d: Blenders can fail, for example from unequal source-gas pressures; the flowmeter is not the usual culprit.

options.a: It is calibrated to 21% and 100% oxygen before each use as directed
options.b: The battery is low, since galvanic cells need battery power to sense
options.c: The fuel cell is depleted or the device is not calibrated to known gases
options.d: It is used on dry gas rather than in a humidified circuit

distractorExplanations.a: Two-point calibration against known gases is what keeps the analyzer accurate; it is not a cause of error.
distractorExplanations.b: Galvanic fuel cells generate their own current; batteries are needed by polarographic analyzers, not galvanic ones.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry gas does not cause error; condensed water on the sensor membrane is what degrades accuracy.

options.a: Warm gas enough to replace the heated humidifier
options.b: Filter bacteria from the expiratory gas
options.c: Cool the gas so more water condenses in the trap
options.d: Reduce condensate in the inspiratory limb

distractorExplanations.a: Heated wires only prevent rainout in the tubing; humidity still has to come from the humidifier chamber.
distractorExplanations.b: Expiratory filters capture bacteria; heated wires manage gas temperature and condensation.
distractorExplanations.c: Heated wires do the opposite: they keep the gas warm so less water condenses in the circuit.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-equipment-004.explanation: Heated wires limit rainout while delivering warm humidified gas to artificial airways. They also keep the humidified gas at the set temperature.

options.a: Circuit disconnection, a cuff leak, or a loose humidifier chamber
options.b: Coughing, secretions, biting, bronchospasm, or decreased compliance
options.c: Increased compliance after diuresis or successful recruitment
options.d: A low set tidal volume combined with a low inspiratory flow

distractorExplanations.a: Disconnections and leaks drop circuit pressure and trigger low-pressure or low-volume alarms instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher compliance lowers the pressure needed per breath, which makes high-pressure alarms less likely.
distractorExplanations.d: Lower tidal volume and flow reduce peak pressure; they do not trigger a high-pressure alarm.

options.a: Sensor drift that requires recalibration against pulse oximetry readings
options.b: Colorimetric detectors turning yellow when exposed to room air
options.c: Sensor contamination, loose connections, and need for periodic zero/span checks
options.d: Reading higher than PaCO2 in healthy lungs, which signals a fault

distractorExplanations.a: Capnographs are zeroed to room air and span-checked with known CO2 gas; pulse oximetry measures oxygenation.
distractorExplanations.b: Colorimetric detectors stay purple in room air and turn yellow when exhaled CO2 is present.
distractorExplanations.d: In healthy lungs ETCO2 normally runs a few mm Hg below PaCO2, so a reading above PaCO2 is not the expected norm.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-equipment-007.explanation: ETCO2 devices require maintenance; waveform interpretation depends on valid sensors. Follow the device's instructions.

options.a: Damage equipment—follow manufacturer sterilization IFUs
options.b: Sterilize the device, so precleaning of soil can be skipped
options.c: Be offset by doubling the exposure time for heat-sensitive plastics
options.d: Only affect metal parts, since plastics tolerate any autoclave cycle

distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning must come before sterilization; residual soil shields microbes and damages surfaces.
distractorExplanations.c: Longer heat or chemical exposure worsens damage to heat-sensitive materials; follow the manufacturer's IFU.
distractorExplanations.d: Many plastics, seals, and electronics are heat- or chemical-sensitive; metal is not the only material at risk.

options.a: Kept in use with the flow raised to make up for the lower purity
options.b: Removed from service and repaired/replaced; verify with analyzer
options.c: Kept in use if the purity alarm resets after a restart
options.d: Kept in use if purity stays above 70 percent at the set flow

distractorExplanations.a: Raising concentrator flow lowers oxygen purity further; the unit must come out of service.
distractorExplanations.c: A reset alarm does not prove purity; output must be verified with an analyzer and the unit repaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Concentrators should deliver roughly 87-95 percent oxygen; 70 percent is far below specification.

options.a: Placing it on the inspiratory side of the circuit so it measures the delivered volume
options.b: Connecting it to a high-flow oxygen source to drive the vane properly
options.c: Proper assembly, leak-free connections, and correct patient technique coaching
options.d: Calibration against a peak flowmeter before each patient measurement

distractorExplanations.a: Wright-type respirometers measure exhaled volume; placement on the expiratory side is standard.
distractorExplanations.b: The patient's exhaled gas drives the vane; no external gas source is connected.
distractorExplanations.d: Volume accuracy is checked with a calibrated syringe, not by comparison with a peak flowmeter.

options.a: Using air flowmeters, which read high, so delivered flow is lower
options.b: Choosing heliox mainly for its higher density to slow airflow
options.c: Using a 70/30 mix for hypoxemic patients who need FiO2 above 0.50
options.d: Correct gas mixture and appropriately calibrated flow devices

distractorExplanations.a: Oxygen and air flowmeters read low with heliox; actual flow is higher (about 1.8 times for 80/20).
distractorExplanations.b: Helium's benefit is its low density, which reduces turbulent flow resistance, not a higher density.
distractorExplanations.c: A 70/30 mix supplies FiO2 0.30; patients needing much more oxygen lose most of the helium benefit.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-equipment-012.explanation: Low-density heliox alters flowmeter behavior and may affect some nebulizers/ventilators. Airway and device compatibility also matter.

options.a: Charge status, vacuum capability, and canister/tubing readiness
options.b: Charge status only, since vacuum level is fixed by the factory
options.c: Canister size and the date of the last biomedical inspection
options.d: Wall vacuum connection, since portable units run on wall suction

distractorExplanations.b: Vacuum capability must be checked by occluding the tubing; it is not guaranteed by the factory setting.
distractorExplanations.c: An inspection sticker is not a function check; charge and vacuum must be verified before transport.
distractorExplanations.d: Battery-powered units exist for transport away from wall vacuum; their own charge and pump are what matter.

options.a: Running controls only when patient results look clinically odd
options.b: Calibrating the analyzer after each sample instead of running controls
options.c: Running control materials, documenting results, and corrective action
options.d: Comparing results against a pulse oximeter reading for each sample

distractorExplanations.a: Controls are run on a set schedule (for example each shift or day), not only when results seem odd.
distractorExplanations.b: Calibration and quality control are separate steps; frequent calibration does not replace running controls.
distractorExplanations.d: SpO2 correlation is a clinical check, not analyzer quality control with assayed control materials.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-equipment-015.explanation: CLIA-style QC principles apply: controls, documentation, and troubleshooting before reporting. Corrective action is taken when controls are out of range.

options.a: Documented hypoxemia or clinical conditions with high risk of hypoxemia
options.b: Dyspnea in any patient, even when SpO2 and PaO2 are normal on room air at rest
options.c: SpO2 below 96 percent in adults with no other risk factors
options.d: Hypercapnia, since oxygen lowers PaCO2 in ventilatory failure

distractorExplanations.b: Dyspnea alone with normal oxygenation is not an AARC indication; therapy targets documented or likely hypoxemia.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypoxemia indications are about PaO2 below 60 mm Hg or SaO2 below 90 percent, not 96 percent.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen does not lower PaCO2; hypercapnia is treated by improving ventilation.

options.a: A precise, fixed FiO2 like an air-entrainment mask
options.b: Moderate FiO2 that varies with fit and flow
options.c: FiO2 near 0.90 when run at 10–15 L/min
options.d: Room-air FiO2 when the flow is set at 5 L/min

distractorExplanations.a: A simple mask is a low-flow, variable-performance device; fixed FiO2 comes from air-entrainment devices.
distractorExplanations.c: FiO2 that high belongs to reservoir or high-flow systems; a simple mask tops out around 0.50-0.60.
distractorExplanations.d: 5 L/min is the minimum flow to flush exhaled CO2 and gives roughly 0.35-0.40, not room air.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-00.explanation: Simple masks provide variable moderate FiO2; NRBs approach higher FiO2 with good fit/flow. Often roughly 0.35–0.50.

options.a: Encourage forced maximal exhalation to measure peak expiratory flow
options.b: Provide positive expiratory pressure to mobilize airway secretions
options.c: Encourage sustained maximal inspiration to prevent/treat atelectasis
options.d: Strengthen expiratory muscles through repeated resisted exhalations

distractorExplanations.a: Forced exhalation for peak flow is asthma monitoring; incentive spirometry trains sustained inspiration.
distractorExplanations.b: Positive expiratory pressure is PEP therapy for secretion clearance, not incentive spirometry.
distractorExplanations.d: Resisted exhalation is expiratory muscle training; incentive spirometry targets deep inspiration.

options.a: Providing inspiratory resistance to strengthen the diaphragm and accessory muscles
options.b: Providing high-frequency oscillation through a vest to loosen secretions
options.c: Delivering positive pressure on inspiration like intermittent positive pressure breathing
options.d: Providing expiratory resistance to stent airways and improve secretion clearance

distractorExplanations.a: Inspiratory resistance is inspiratory muscle training; PEP applies resistance during exhalation.
distractorExplanations.b: Vest oscillation is high-frequency chest wall compression, a different airway clearance device.
distractorExplanations.c: Positive pressure on inspiration describes IPPB; PEP works by resisting exhalation.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-00.explanation: PEP/OPEP devices aid airway clearance adjunctively with coughing and hydration as appropriate. It can also aid recruitment.

options.a: Tidal volumes of 10–12 mL/kg actual body weight to recruit alveoli
options.b: Lower tidal volumes (e.g., ~6 mL/kg PBW) and limited plateau pressures
options.c: Normal PaCO2 at all times, even if plateau pressure must exceed 30
options.d: Low tidal volumes with PEEP kept at zero to limit barotrauma

distractorExplanations.a: ARDSNet uses 4-8 mL/kg of predicted body weight; actual weight and 10-12 mL/kg overdistend the lung.
distractorExplanations.c: Permissive hypercapnia is accepted to keep plateau pressure at or below about 30 cm H2O.
distractorExplanations.d: PEEP is part of lung-protective ventilation to prevent derecruitment; zero PEEP worsens shunt.

options.a: Long-acting β2-agonist bronchodilator
options.b: Short-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator
options.c: Short-acting β2-agonist bronchodilator
options.d: Inhaled corticosteroid controller agent

distractorExplanations.a: Albuterol is short-acting; salmeterol and formoterol are the long-acting β2-agonists.
distractorExplanations.b: The short-acting anticholinergic is ipratropium; albuterol acts on β2 receptors.
distractorExplanations.d: Inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone are controllers; albuterol is a rescue bronchodilator.

options.a: Thin mucus by breaking DNA strands in purulent sputum
options.b: Break disulfide bonds in mucus as a mucolytic agent
options.c: Reduce airway inflammation as a steroid substitute
options.d: Hydrate airway mucus and facilitate clearance

distractorExplanations.a: Breaking extracellular DNA in purulent sputum is how dornase alfa works, not hypertonic saline.
distractorExplanations.b: Breaking disulfide bonds is acetylcysteine's mechanism; hypertonic saline works osmotically.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypertonic saline has no corticosteroid action and can cause bronchospasm; it hydrates the airway surface.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-00.explanation: Hypertonic saline is an airway clearance adjunct in appropriate protocols—not systemic sodium repair via nebulizer intent. It is used in select CF care pathways.

options.a: Hypotension and barotrauma in susceptible patients
options.b: Hypertension from increased venous return to the heart
options.c: Bradycardia and pulmonary edema from lowered pleural pressure
options.d: Increased cardiac output from improved oxygenation

distractorExplanations.b: Raised intrathoracic pressure decreases venous return, which causes hypotension rather than hypertension.
distractorExplanations.c: Recruitment and high PEEP raise pleural pressure; the main risks are hypotension and barotrauma.
distractorExplanations.d: High intrathoracic pressure usually lowers cardiac output by reducing preload.

options.a: Lower plateau pressure enough to allow higher tidal volumes
options.b: Improve oxygenation by redistributing perfusion/ventilation
options.c: Improve secretion drainage as the primary goal of the therapy
options.d: Reduce the need for sedation during mechanical ventilation

distractorExplanations.a: Proning is used with low tidal volumes; it is not a way to justify larger tidal volumes.
distractorExplanations.c: Secretion drainage is a side benefit; prone positioning is used mainly to improve oxygenation.
distractorExplanations.d: Prone positioning often requires deep sedation and sometimes paralysis, not less sedation.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-01.explanation: Proning can improve V/Q in severe ARDS; teams manage lines, airway, and pressure points. This works in many patients.

options.a: Placing the nebulizer at the Y-piece with bias flow running at its highest setting
options.b: Leaving the HME in place between the nebulizer and the patient
options.c: Optimal nebulizer/MDI adapter placement, synchronizing when appropriate
options.d: Increasing humidification to maximum, since humid gas boosts particle delivery

distractorExplanations.a: High bias flow washes aerosol into the expiratory limb; bias flow is reduced during nebulization.
distractorExplanations.b: An HME traps aerosol particles; it must be removed or bypassed during in-line aerosol delivery.
distractorExplanations.d: Humidified gas enlarges particles and lowers deposition; humidity reduces, not boosts, delivery.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-01.explanation: Device position and ventilator interactions affect inhaled dose; follow evidence-based aerosol practices. Minimizing circuit losses per best practice also helps.

options.a: Cystic fibrosis with thick secretions and frequent exacerbations
options.b: Lobar atelectasis caused by mucus plugging after surgery
options.c: Bronchiectasis with daily sputum production over 30 mL
options.d: Active hemoptysis, unstable spinal injury, or untreated pneumothorax

distractorExplanations.a: Cystic fibrosis with retained secretions is a core indication for chest physiotherapy, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.b: Atelectasis from mucus plugging is an indication for postural drainage and percussion.
distractorExplanations.c: Sputum production over about 25-30 mL per day is an indication for chest physiotherapy.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-01.explanation: External maneuvers can worsen bleeding, fractures, or air leaks—screen contraindications. These are classic cautions.

options.a: Assist removal of retained secretions and improve ventilation/perfusion
options.b: Reverse bronchospasm by relaxing airway smooth muscle directly with each treatment
options.c: Prevent atelectasis by sustained maximal inspiration alone
options.d: Reduce airway inflammation and mucus production over time

distractorExplanations.b: Relaxing airway smooth muscle is the goal of bronchodilators, not bronchial hygiene therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Sustained maximal inspiration is lung expansion therapy such as incentive spirometry.
distractorExplanations.d: Reducing inflammation is the role of inhaled corticosteroids; bronchial hygiene removes secretions.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-01.explanation: Clearance therapies target mucus plugging/retention—not structural fibrosis cure or unsafe ICP rises. This matters where secretions impair gas exchange.

options.a: Target SpO2 of 94–98 percent, as for other adult patients
options.b: Target appropriate SpO2 goals and monitor ventilation/ABG
options.c: Avoid oxygen until an ABG confirms the PaCO2 level
options.d: Use a nonrebreather to keep SpO2 at 100 percent

distractorExplanations.a: Patients at risk of hypercapnic failure usually get a lower target of about 88-92 percent.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygen should not be withheld from a hypoxemic patient while waiting for an ABG.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperoxia in these patients can worsen hypercapnia; oxygen is titrated to a target range.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-therapeutics-01.explanation: Titrate to goals (often ~88–92% in at-risk COPD per many protocols) while watching for CO2 retention/clinical decline. Monitor as clinically indicated.

options.a: Measure airway resistance before and after bronchodilator use
options.b: Strengthen inspiratory muscles before ventilator weaning
options.c: Mobilize secretions as part of an airway clearance program
options.d: Replace the need for patient coughing to clear secretions

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchodilator response is measured with pulmonary function testing, not airway clearance devices.
distractorExplanations.b: Building inspiratory strength is inspiratory muscle training, not IPV or chest wall oscillation.
distractorExplanations.d: These devices loosen secretions, but coughing or suctioning is still needed to remove them.

options.a: Activate emergency response and begin CAB/ABCs
options.b: Check a carotid pulse for a full 30 seconds
options.c: Give two rescue breaths before calling for help
options.d: Apply oxygen by nonrebreather and recheck in 1 minute

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds or less so compressions are not delayed.
distractorExplanations.c: For an unresponsive adult, help is activated first and adult CPR follows the CAB sequence.
distractorExplanations.d: An apneic patient needs ventilation and CPR as indicated; passive oxygen does nothing without breathing.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-001.explanation: Basic life support priorities precede advanced diagnostics in arrest/near-arrest. Open the airway and provide ventilation or CPR as indicated.

options.a: A chest X-ray to confirm before any intervention
options.b: Immediate decompression per emergency protocol
options.c: Increasing PEEP to re-expand the collapsed lung
options.d: A 12-lead ECG to rule out cardiac tamponade

distractorExplanations.a: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays lifesaving decompression.
distractorExplanations.c: Added positive pressure enlarges a tension pneumothorax and worsens hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Tracheal deviation with hypotension points to tension pneumothorax; an ECG delays decompression.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-002.explanation: Tension physiology is immediately life-threatening; decompression is the priority. Support oxygenation and ventilation.

options.a: Back blows only, since thrusts injure adult patients
options.b: Encouraging forceful coughing until the object clears
options.c: Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) or approved protocol
options.d: A blind finger sweep followed by rescue breaths

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts are the recommended adult response for severe obstruction despite injury risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Coughing is encouraged in mild obstruction; severe signs (cannot speak or cough) need thrusts.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are not recommended.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-003.explanation: Severe FBAO needs immediate dislodgement maneuvers per BLS guidelines. Continue until expulsion or the patient becomes unresponsive.

options.a: Ventilation rate increases, washing more CO2 out of the lungs
options.b: Epinephrine raises CO2 production in the tissues
options.c: The ETT has moved from the esophagus into the trachea
options.d: Pulmonary blood flow resumes and delivers CO2 to the lungs

distractorExplanations.a: Faster ventilation lowers ETCO2; the abrupt rise at ROSC reflects restored pulmonary perfusion.
distractorExplanations.b: Epinephrine can transiently lower ETCO2; the sudden rise at ROSC comes from restored blood flow.
distractorExplanations.c: An esophageal tube reads near zero throughout; the ROSC rise occurs with a correctly placed tube.

options.a: Airway support with BVM and preparation for reintubation as needed
options.b: Immediate reintubation without first oxygenating the patient
options.c: High-flow nasal cannula at 60 L/min and reassess in an hour
options.d: A nonrebreather mask and an ABG before any airway decision

distractorExplanations.b: The patient is oxygenated and ventilated with a BVM first; rushing reintubation risks hypoxemia.
distractorExplanations.c: Inadequate breathing needs assisted ventilation; high-flow cannula does not ventilate the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for an ABG delays needed ventilation; inadequate breathing calls for BVM support now.

options.a: Switching from sevoflurane to desflurane and continuing the case
options.b: Stopping triggering agents and hyperventilating with 100% O2
options.c: Reducing minute ventilation to let PaCO2 rise and stimulate breathing
options.d: Giving succinylcholine to relieve the muscle rigidity quickly

distractorExplanations.a: All volatile anesthetics trigger malignant hyperthermia; switching agents does not remove the trigger.
distractorExplanations.c: MH drives CO2 production up; minute ventilation is increased to clear CO2, not reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: Succinylcholine is itself an MH trigger; dantrolene is the treatment for rigidity.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-006.explanation: MH is a hypermetabolic emergency; anesthesia teams lead dantrolene protocols while RTs support ventilation/cooling logistics. Support dantrolene and protocol care.

options.a: Increasing EPAP to 15 to keep NPPV going
options.b: Switching to high-flow nasal cannula
options.c: Need for intubation/mechanical ventilation
options.d: Adding heliox and continuing NPPV overnight

distractorExplanations.a: Exhaustion on NPPV signals failure; raising settings and continuing delays needed intubation.
distractorExplanations.b: High-flow cannula gives less ventilatory support than NPPV and cannot rescue an exhausted patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Heliox can bridge some patients, but exhaustion means intubation now rather than continuing overnight.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-007.explanation: Fatigue/hypercapnia despite maximal therapy indicates invasive support; vent strategies allow exhalation. Use a ventilator strategy that avoids air trapping.

options.a: Positioning the bleeding side up to drain blood out of it
options.b: Chest physiotherapy to clear clots from the bleeding lung
options.c: Incentive spirometry to keep the bleeding lung expanded
options.d: Airway protection (often bleeding side down) and oxygenation

distractorExplanations.a: Bleeding side up lets blood spill into the good lung; the bleeding side goes down.
distractorExplanations.b: Percussion and drainage are contraindicated in active hemoptysis and can worsen bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Lung expansion therapy is not a priority; the airway and oxygenation come first in massive hemoptysis.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-008.explanation: Protect the airway and non-bleeding lung; control bleeding with specialist care. Then activate urgent team and bronchoscopy pathways.

options.a: Stop ventilation/gases as protocol directs, remove burning tube, extinguish
options.b: Increase FiO2 to 1.0 and keep ventilating through the tube
options.c: Leave the tube in place and flush it with saline while continuing to ventilate with oxygen
options.d: Stop the laser and continue ventilation with nitrous oxide

distractorExplanations.b: Oxygen feeds an airway fire; gas flow is stopped and the burning tube removed.
distractorExplanations.c: The burning tube is removed and ventilation stopped; ventilating through it keeps feeding the fire.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitrous oxide supports combustion as strongly as oxygen; all gas flow is stopped.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-009.explanation: Airway fire algorithms prioritize removing the fuel/oxidizer source and protecting the patient. Then re-establish the airway and oxygenation.

options.a: Increasing the set rate to shorten each breath and reduce trapping
options.b: Temporarily disconnecting to allow exhalation / lowering rate and I:E adjustments
options.c: Adding applied PEEP well above the measured auto-PEEP level to splint the airways open
options.d: Increasing tidal volume and inspiratory time to improve CO2 removal and oxygenation

distractorExplanations.a: A higher rate shortens expiratory time and increases auto-PEEP; the rate is lowered instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Applied PEEP above the intrinsic level adds to hyperinflation and worsens hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Larger volumes and longer inspiration leave less time to exhale and increase air trapping.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-010.explanation: Severe air trapping impairs venous return; allow exhalation and adjust settings. Follow protocol.

options.a: Diphenhydramine IV as the first-line drug, then reassess
options.b: Methylprednisolone IV to stop the reaction within minutes
options.c: Epinephrine IM (per protocol) and airway/oxygen support
options.d: Epinephrine IV push of 1 mg (1:1,000) as the first dose

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines are adjuncts; IM epinephrine is the first-line drug in anaphylaxis.
distractorExplanations.b: Corticosteroids take hours to act and are not first-line; epinephrine is.
distractorExplanations.d: A 1 mg IV bolus is cardiac-arrest dosing; first-line anaphylaxis dosing is about 0.3-0.5 mg IM.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-011.explanation: IM epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis; airway support is concurrent. Activate the emergency response.

options.a: Bronchospasm, treated first with a bronchodilator nebulizer
options.b: Cuff leak, treated by adding air to the ETT pilot balloon
options.c: Pulmonary edema from the line's fluid bolus, treated with diuretics
options.d: Mainstem intubation or pneumothorax—assess, auscultate, adjust tube depth

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchospasm causes bilateral wheeze and high pressures, not asymmetric chest rise.
distractorExplanations.b: A cuff leak causes audible leak and low volumes, not one-sided chest rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulmonary edema gives bilateral crackles; asymmetric chest rise points to tube position or pneumothorax.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-012.explanation: Acute asymmetry after intubation/central lines demands rapid differentiation of tube malposition vs PTX. Image or decompress as indicated.

options.a: Ventilatory support if arrest/respiratory failure occurs
options.b: Albuterol by nebulizer as the definitive way to remove potassium
options.c: Hypoventilation to raise PaCO2 and drive potassium into cells
options.d: Sodium bicarbonate nebulization to lower serum potassium

distractorExplanations.b: Albuterol shifts potassium into cells temporarily; it does not remove potassium from the body.
distractorExplanations.c: Respiratory acidosis moves potassium out of cells; alkalosis is what shifts it in.
distractorExplanations.d: Bicarbonate is given IV when used; it is not a nebulized respiratory therapy for hyperkalemia.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-013.explanation: RTs manage airway/ventilation emergencies while medical teams shift/remove potassium. Medical therapy (calcium, shifts) proceeds alongside.

options.a: Giving every patient 15 L/min by nonrebreather until supplies run out
options.b: Titrating O2 to clinically appropriate targets and conserving resources
options.c: Allocating oxygen first-come, first-served as patients arrive
options.d: Reserving cylinders for ventilated patients and stopping all others

distractorExplanations.a: Untitrated maximal flow exhausts supply quickly; oxygen is titrated to targets in a mass-casualty event.
distractorExplanations.c: Allocation follows triage by need and likely benefit, not arrival order.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-ventilated hypoxemic patients still need titrated oxygen; triage frameworks guide allocation.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-014.explanation: Crisis standards still aim for best outcomes with limited O2—assessment and titration matter. Use triage frameworks.

options.a: Repeated direct laryngoscopy attempts until the tube passes, then oxygenating
options.b: Proceeding straight to a surgical airway after the first failed laryngoscopy attempt by anyone
options.c: Oxygenation first, calling for help, and progressing through established failed-airway pathways
options.d: Paralyzing again and trying blind nasal intubation before calling for help

distractorExplanations.a: Attempts are limited and oxygenation is maintained between them; repeated attempts cause airway trauma.
distractorExplanations.b: A surgical airway is for a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate situation after BVM or supraglottic rescue fails.
distractorExplanations.d: Help is called early; blind nasal attempts are not part of standard failed-airway pathways.

nbrc-tmc-readiness-check-emergency-015.explanation: Cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate pathways emphasize oxygen, help, and rescue devices/cricothyrotomy. This includes a surgical airway when needed.
